analysis.one_liner: Rewrites energy tax law to reward clean power and efficiency while ending oil and gas tax breaks.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill; after it was placed on the Senate calendar in June 2021, no committee or floor action followed before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would consolidate decades of scattered energy tax breaks into a simpler set of credits: a per-kilowatt-hour production credit and a 30% investment credit for any power facility with zero greenhouse-gas emissions, a 30% credit for rooftop solar and home batteries, credits for clean vehicles, clean fuels, and hydrogen, and improved credits for energy-efficient homes and commercial buildings. It would repeal a set of oil and gas tax provisions, and it would require companies claiming the big credits to pay construction workers local prevailing wages and to fill at least 15% of project labor hours with registered apprentices. The credits would phase out once US power-sector emissions fell to a quarter of 2021 levels.
analysis.who_benefits: Households buying rooftop solar, home batteries, or efficiency upgrades would get a 30% tax credit that counts installation labor; clean-power builders would get long-term production and investment credits with bonuses for projects in former coal communities and for using American-made components; construction workers on those projects would be guaranteed prevailing wages and apprentice hours; and states, rural co-ops, and tribal governments could receive the credits as direct payments rather than tax offsets. Air quality in power-producing regions would improve as zero-emission generation replaced fossil generation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households, clean-energy builders, and construction workers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a 1.5-cent-per-kilowatt-hour production credit (inflation-adjusted, 10-year window) and a 30% investment credit for electricity facilities with a zero greenhouse-gas emissions rate, plus credits for energy storage and transmission property.

Creates a 30% residential clean electricity credit for solar and home battery systems used at a principal residence, including the cost of on-site installation labor, with a three-year carryforward for households that cannot use the full credit in one year.

Requires any laborers and mechanics on projects claiming the major credits to be paid local prevailing wages, imposes a $5,000-per-worker penalty for violations, and requires at least 15% of total workforce labor hours to be performed by qualified apprentices.

Adds a 10% bonus credit for facilities in 'energy communities' — census tracts near closed coal mines, retired coal plants, or heavy oil-and-gas employment — and for projects meeting domestic content requirements for US-produced steel, iron, and manufactured products.

Lets state utilities with a service obligation, rural electric cooperatives, and Indian tribal governments elect to receive the credits as direct payments, since these entities often have little tax liability to offset.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the credits, which the bill does not offset with new revenue beyond the fossil-fuel repeals. Oil and gas companies would lose long-standing tax provisions. Because the home credits require buying equipment upfront, the household benefits would flow disproportionately to property owners who can afford the initial investment, while renters and lower-income families would see less of it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, and oil and gas companies

drawbacks.text: The bill's new credits are not paid for: beyond repealing certain oil and gas provisions, the bill contains no revenue offset, so its full cost would be added to the federal deficit unless paired with other legislation.

The residential credit rewards households that can finance upfront purchases of solar and battery equipment; renters and families without the cash or credit to install systems would get little direct benefit, so the household-side gains would skew toward better-off homeowners.

The bill's emissions-rate machinery is complex: the Treasury Secretary and EPA would have to set emissions rates by facility category, handle petitions and provisional rates, and issue final guidance by January 2023, leaving considerable room for disputes over which facilities qualify.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-side design is unusually strong for a tax bill: public money flows only to projects paying area prevailing wages with apprentice hours, the credits are technology-neutral and phase out as emissions fall, and former coal communities get a bonus. The real cost is fiscal — the bill pays for only a fraction of itself — and the household credits tilt toward owners who can invest upfront. On balance the bill would spend public money to build clean generation and cut household energy bills, with the wage standards ensuring much of the spending reaches workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and placed directly on the Senate calendar in June 2021, but no committee ever acted on it and no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the Clean Energy for America Act on June 17, 2021, with nine Democratic cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 78) on June 21, 2021 — bypassing an initial committee referral.
No further action of any kind was recorded after June 21, 2021; the bill received no hearing, no committee markup, and no floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
All ten senators who sponsored or cosponsored the bill were Democrats; none of the 50 Senate Republicans signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers kept the tax provisions the bill would have repealed. Clean-energy developers and households got nothing from this bill itself; the credits it proposed never became law through this route during the 117th Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers kept their tax breaks

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.role: US Senator from Oregon; Chairman, Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill, drafting the tax-credit framework through the committee he chairs.

for.name: 9 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Stabenow, Menendez, Carper, Cardin, Brown, Bennet, Casey, Whitehouse, Cortez Masto)

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; after it was placed on the calendar in June 2021, no vote was ever scheduled during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic: 10 Senate Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill and none of the 50 Senate Republicans did, and the bill never drew a floor vote in either direction.

industries.note: The bill terminates certain oil, gas, and fossil fuel tax provisions and attaches wage penalties to the credits that remain, directly clawing back longstanding industry tax breaks. Industry revenue from these provisions would end if it passed.

A 1.5-cent production credit and 30% investment credit for zero-emission power facilities, storage, and transmission, with bonuses for domestic content and coal-community locations. These companies profit by building the clean generation the bill aims to produce, so their gain runs alongside the public's.

industries.industry: Electric utilities, cooperatives, and grid operators
industries.note: Credits cover energy storage and transmission property, and state utilities, rural co-ops, and tribal governments can take direct payments instead of tax offsets. Lower-carbon, better-invested grids serve customers directly.
A 30% credit for rooftop solar, home batteries, and efficiency upgrades — including installation labor — would drive household demand for these companies' work while lowering buyers' energy bills.

industries.industry: Carbon capture and direct air capture developers
industries.note: The bill raises the carbon capture credit to $175-$150 per ton for direct air capture, requires high capture rates for qualified facilities, ends use of captured CO2 for enhanced oil recovery after 2026, and allows tax-exempt bonds for CO2 capture facilities. Public benefit depends on whether captured carbon is genuinely stored rather than used to pump more oil.
